name: Semantic Externalism
statement: What your words and thoughts mean depends partly on your environment, not just what is in your head.
statementAccent: not just what is in your head
meaning: Semantic externalism, also called content externalism or anti-individualism, is the thesis that the meanings of a person's words, and the contents of their thoughts, are not determined solely by what is going on inside their head, their intrinsic psychological states, but depend partly on features of their external environment, the physical world or the social and linguistic community. Its slogan, from Hilary Putnam, is that meanings just ain't in the head. It is opposed to internalism, or individualism, on which content is fixed by internal states alone, so-called narrow content. The most famous argument for externalism is Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment, from his 1975 paper The Meaning of Meaning. Imagine Twin Earth, identical to Earth except that the clear, drinkable liquid there called water is not H2O but a different chemical, XYZ, superficially indistinguishable. Set the case in about 1750, before anyone knew water's molecular structure, and consider a person on Earth and their molecule-for-molecule identical twin on Twin Earth: they are in the very same internal brain states, yet the Earth speaker's word water refers to H2O and the twin's water refers to XYZ. So meaning differs despite identical internal states, showing that reference depends on the environment. Putnam also stressed the division of linguistic labor, and Tyler Burge extended externalism to a wide range of concepts through social externalism.
mechanism: Semantic externalism works by showing that two individuals could be internally identical while their words and thoughts differ in meaning or content, which entails that content is not fixed by the inside alone. Putnam's Twin Earth case supplies the argument: the Earthling and the Twin-Earthling are perfect internal duplicates, sharing all narrow psychological states, yet because the stuff each has actually interacted with and been embedded among is different, H2O here and XYZ there, their term water refers to different substances, and their thoughts about water have different contents. What makes the difference is the environment, not anything in the head. Putnam added the division of linguistic labor: ordinary speakers can use terms like gold, elm, or aluminum and refer correctly even if they cannot themselves tell what really falls under the term, because they defer to experts in the community who can, so that reference is a collective, social achievement rather than a matter of each speaker's private descriptive knowledge. Tyler Burge, in his 1979 paper Individualism and the Mental, generalized externalism to ordinary concepts through social externalism, using the arthritis thought experiment: a person who mistakenly believes they have arthritis in the thigh has a concept whose content is fixed by their community's use of the word, and a counterfactual person with identical internal states in a community where arthritis meant something broader would have a different concept. In each case the content of thought and language reaches out into the world and the community.

examples.text: An Earthling and their identical twin on Twin Earth, in the same brain states, mean H2O and XYZ by water, so meaning depends on the environment.
A speaker who cannot tell elms from beeches still refers to elms by deferring to experts, making reference a social achievement.
A person's concept arthritis is fixed by their community's usage, so identical inner states in a different community yield a different concept.

variants.name: Physical externalism
variants.text: Putnam's Twin Earth externalism, on which the physical nature of the environment helps fix the reference of natural kind terms.

variants.name: Social externalism
variants.text: Burge's anti-individualism, on which the linguistic community's usage helps fix the contents of many ordinary concepts.

whyItMatters: Semantic externalism is one of the most consequential positions in the philosophy of language and mind, overturning the long-standing Cartesian assumption that the contents of our thoughts and the meanings of our words are wholly determined by what lies inside us. Putnam's Twin Earth and the slogan that meanings ain't in the head, together with Burge's arthritis case, made a compelling argument that content depends partly on the physical environment and the linguistic community, so that two internally identical people can mean and think different things. This reshaped debates about meaning, reference, and mental content, and it dovetails with the causal theory of reference, since both locate the determination of reference outside the individual's descriptive knowledge, in causal and social relations to the world. Externalism also poses a sharp challenge to the traditional idea of privileged self-knowledge: if the contents of one's own thoughts are partly fixed by the environment, it can seem that knowing one's own mind might require knowing about the world, generating the much-debated tension between externalism and self-knowledge. The view has ramifications for the theory of mind, epistemology, and cognitive science. As the thesis that meaning and thought reach beyond the head into the world, semantic externalism is a landmark development.

working.text: imagine two people in identical internal psychological states, as in Twin Earth or the arthritis case.
let their physical environment or linguistic community differ while their inner states stay the same.
note that their words and thoughts differ in content, so meaning depends partly on the environment, not the head alone.

limits: Semantic externalism is widely accepted but not uncontested, and it raises hard problems. Internalists resist it, defending a notion of narrow content fixed by internal states, and argue that there is a psychologically important kind of content the Twin Earth cases leave untouched, since the duplicates are alike in how things seem to them and in the causal role of their states. A central difficulty is the apparent conflict with privileged self-knowledge: if content is partly environmental, it can seem that one could not know one's own thoughts by introspection alone without also knowing about the environment, a worry sharpened by slow-switching arguments, and much effort has gone into showing externalism and self-knowledge are compatible. There are also questions about how far externalism extends, whether it applies to all concepts or only to natural kind and socially deferential terms, and about the details of the thought experiments. Some specifics reward care: the entry that treats this material is titled Externalism About the Mind despite its URL, the division of linguistic labor is Putnam's but is not covered in every source, and the twins names vary across retellings. So semantic externalism robustly shows that content depends partly on the environment, understood as an influential thesis pressed by internalists and by worries about self-knowledge.
misreadings: Semantic externalism is not the claim that internal states play no role in meaning; it claims they do not by themselves fix content, which also depends on the environment. It does not deny that we know our own minds, only that reconciling such knowledge with externalism requires care, since content is partly world-involving. And Twin Earth is a thought experiment about reference, not a claim that a substance like XYZ actually exists, so treating externalism as ignoring the inner, as denying self-knowledge outright, or as positing real XYZ, misreads the thesis.
origin: The thesis, argued by Hilary Putnam via the Twin Earth thought experiment (1975) and extended by Tyler Burge to social content (1979), that the meanings of words and the contents of thoughts depend partly on the external environment and community.

sources.text: Externalism About the Mind, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — content externalism as the thesis that mental content depends on the nature of the environment beyond the individual, Putnam's Twin Earth and the H2O versus XYZ case set around 1750, Burge's arthritis thought experiment and social externalism, and the challenge to privileged self-knowledge.

Internalism and Externalism in the Philosophy of Mind and Language, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the internalism-externalism contrast, narrow versus world-involving content, the causal individuation of content, and the self-knowledge worry.
